intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. The notes under each slide explain it, tell you what to remember and warn you where people slip. Work the examples in pencil before you read the steps, and answer the recall questions from memory.

sections.title: What Is Development Economics?
sections.big_idea: Development economics asks why countries prosper or stall, and it **drops the assumption that markets simply work**.
in_plain_words: The field studies the economic, social and institutional change of low- and middle-income countries. It joins macro questions such as growth and trade to micro questions about households, firms and credit. What sets it apart is that markets are often missing or thin, information is uneven and history shapes what is possible.

Three traditions shape it: structure and institutions, experiments, and capabilities. Sen ties them together by defining development as the real freedoms people enjoy, with income as one means to them. **Use all three** when you analyse a programme, because the deck says no single tradition is sufficient.

left.title: Standard economics
items: Markets assumed to work reasonably well

right.title: Development economics
items: Markets often missing, thin or distorted

key_terms.meaning: Study of economic, social and institutional change in low- and middle-income countries.
Sen's view that development expands what people can be and do.
Past events such as colonial rule or land reform shape outcomes today.
Moving resources from low-productivity farming to industry and services.
A market that is missing, thin or distorted, so it allocates badly.

worked_example.title: Match each claim to a tradition
worked_example.setup: A colleague makes three claims about a district. Which tradition does each draw on?
steps: Claim 1: farm labour should move into factories and services. That is the structural and institutional tradition (Lewis).
Claim 2: run a randomised trial before scaling the programme. That is the experimental tradition (Banerjee and Duflo).
Claim 3: judge success by health, schooling and voice, with GDP as a means. That is the capabilities tradition (Sen).
worked_example.answer: Structural, experimental, capabilities. A strong analysis draws on all three.

mistakes: Treating development economics as standard economics applied to poorer places, and assuming credit, information and contracts work.
Equating development with GDP growth. Sen's test is whether people's real freedoms expand.
Picking one tradition and ignoring the other two. The deck says none is sufficient alone.

recall.q: What is the core question of the field?
recall.a: Why some countries grow rich while others remain poor, and what governments and practitioners can do about it.

recall.q: Name the three major traditions.
recall.a: Structural and institutional; experimental and micro-empirical; capabilities and human development.

recall.q: Which pair won the 2019 Nobel with the experimental approach?
recall.a: Banerjee and Duflo, together with Michael Kremer.

recall.q: How does Sen define development?
recall.a: As a process of expanding the real freedoms that people enjoy.

sections.title: Measuring Development
sections.big_idea: No single number measures development, so **triangulate** income, deprivation, distribution and qualitative evidence.
in_plain_words: GDP per capita is easy to compare and tracks life expectancy and literacy, but it ignores distribution, unpaid work, environmental costs and wellbeing. The HDI adds health and education to income through a geometric mean of three indices, which is how Bangladesh could rank above Pakistan on HDI with a lower income.

Poverty lines and the MPI measure deprivation in different ways. Any monetary line is arbitrary, and the MPI depends on its own thresholds. The Gini summarises distribution, and **wealth Ginis run far higher than income Ginis**. For any figure, ask which measure it is, who produced it and what it leaves out.

diagram.note: the HDI is the geometric mean of the three normalised indices

key_terms.meaning: Adjusts for price level differences so incomes compare across countries.
UNDP index combining health, education and income, scored 0 to 1.
Counts people deprived in at least one-third of weighted indicators at once.
0 means perfect equality and 1 means one person owns everything.
Plots the actual distribution against the 45 degree equality line.

worked_example.title: Weight of one MPI indicator
worked_example.setup: Work out how much one living standards indicator counts in the MPI.
steps: Each of the three dimensions carries a weight of one-third: 1 ÷ 3 = 0.333.
Living standards has six indicators sharing that third equally, so each carries 1 ÷ 18 = 0.056.
Check the six together: 6 × 0.056 = 0.336, which rounds back to one-third.
A household deprived in all six reaches the cut-off on that dimension alone: 6 ÷ 18 = 0.333.
worked_example.answer: Each living standards indicator weighs 1/18, about 0.056, and all six together make one-third.

mistakes: Comparing poverty counts across countries without a PPP adjustment.
Quoting a Gini without saying whether it is income or wealth. India's are 0.35 and 0.63.
Using GDP growth to claim development progress. India's growth averaged over 7% while female participation fell.
Quoting India's poverty as current. The last comparable consumption survey is 2011-12.

recall.q: Which three indices make up the HDI?
recall.a: Health (life expectancy), education (schooling years) and income (GNI per capita in PPP).

recall.q: What is the MPI poverty cut-off on slide 14?
recall.a: Deprivation in at least one-third of the weighted indicators across health, education and living standards.

recall.q: Name two things GDP cannot capture.
recall.a: Any two of: distribution, unpaid work, environmental costs, the informal economy, non-market services, wellbeing.

recall.q: Why is India's poverty estimate uncertain?
recall.a: No full consumption survey since 2011-12; the 2017-18 round was suppressed and 2022-23 changed method.

recall.q: What does a wealth Gini above an income Gini tell you?
recall.a: Assets such as land, financial holdings and businesses are far more concentrated than income.

sections.title: Poverty & Inequality
sections.big_idea: Poverty persists because **its own mechanisms trap people**: weak assets, shocks and exclusion pass from parents to children.
in_plain_words: A poverty trap is a self-reinforcing loop. Low income means low savings, little investment in children and low adult productivity. In the S-curve model there are two stable equilibria, one poor and one rich, with an unstable threshold between them, so a large enough one-time push can have a permanent effect.

In India poverty is patterned by caste, gender, land and geography, so the poor are many groups. Social protection tools such as the PDS, the employment guarantee and cash transfers act as floors, and the evidence differs by instrument. **Ask who the design leaves out** as well as who it reaches.

diagram.caption: the loop that repeats across generations

key_terms.meaning: Self-reinforcing mechanism that stops the poor making the investments needed to escape.
Hypothesis that inequality rises then falls with development; the evidence is weak.
How closely a child's income tracks the parent's.
Childcare, elder care and housework, mostly done by women and left out of GDP.
The state as employer of last resort, as in MGNREGS.

worked_example.title: How persistent is India?
worked_example.setup: The deck gives an intergenerational income elasticity of 0.52 for India and 0.15 for the Nordic countries. The last step uses an illustrative national poverty rate.
steps: India is 0.52 and the Nordic countries are 0.15.
Divide India by the Nordic figure: 0.52 ÷ 0.15 = 3.47.
A parent's income advantage carries over to the child about 3.5 times as strongly in India.
ST poverty is 2.3 times the national headcount. With an illustrative national rate of 20%, 2.3 × 20 = 46%.
worked_example.answer: India's elasticity is about 3.5 times the Nordic figure, and an ST headcount 2.3 times a 20% national rate is 46%.

mistakes: Reading the Kuznets curve as a law. The slide says cross-country data shows no clear inverted U.
Taking household poverty rates as each person's experience. Women and girls often eat last and leave school first.
Treating the rural poor as one group. They include landless labourers, marginal farmers, SC and ST households and more.
Expecting a one-time intervention to last when the underlying mechanisms stay in place.

recall.q: What does the S-curve model say about a one-time push?
recall.a: Pushing households across the unstable threshold can have permanent effects.

recall.q: Which states hold over half of India's poor?
recall.a: Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand and Odisha, with Rajasthan added on slide 23.

recall.q: How do poor people describe poverty in Voices of the Poor?
recall.a: They rarely start with income and talk about insecurity, voicelessness, powerlessness and humiliation.

recall.q: Name two social protection instruments and their Indian programmes.
recall.a: Food subsidy through NFSA and the PDS; employment guarantee through MGNREGS.

recall.q: What was India's female labour force participation rate in 2022 (CMIE)?

sections.title: Growth Models & Structural Transformation
sections.big_idea: Growth theory moves from capital to ideas to institutions, and India's path **skipped the manufacturing step**.
in_plain_words: Solow explains growth through capital and labour with diminishing returns, so only technology lifts the long-run rate. Romer and Lucas make technology the result of investment in ideas and human capital. Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson add institutions as the deep determinant, shaped by colonial history.

Lewis describes labour moving from surplus-labour farming to a modern sector. India moved to services and bypassed manufacturing, so mass employment did not follow. Policy moved from the Washington Consensus to context-specific diagnosis and a return of industrial policy. **Judge growth by the jobs it creates.**

events.what: AJR link settler mortality to institutions

diagram.caption: seven dates behind the growth debate

key_terms.meaning: Output growth unexplained by capital and labour, driven by technology and institutions.
Poor countries catch up only with similar savings, institutions and technology access.
When surplus labour is used up and agricultural wages start to rise.
Growth from deliberate investment in knowledge and human capital.
Ten-point IMF and World Bank reform package of the 1980s and 1990s.

worked_example.title: How much growth is TFP?
worked_example.setup: Use the Solow figures from the deck with an illustrative rich-country growth rate of 2% a year.
steps: The capital share α is about 0.33, so labour's exponent is 1 − 0.33 = 0.67.
The deck says 50% to 70% of growth in rich countries is unexplained by capital and labour.
At 50%: 2 × 0.5 = 1 percentage point of growth is TFP.
At 70%: 2 × 0.7 = 1.4 percentage points.
worked_example.answer: Between 1 and 1.4 of the 2 percentage points of growth would be TFP.

mistakes: Reading Solow as saying saving drives long-run growth. A higher saving rate raises the level of output only.
Assuming poor countries always catch up. Convergence holds conditionally.
Treating India's 1991 reforms as the full Washington Consensus. The slide calls them partial.
Reading India's growth as job creation. It was capital and skill intensive.

recall.q: What does the Solow residual capture?
recall.a: Growth unexplained by capital and labour, called TFP, driven by technology and institutions.

recall.q: What is the Lewis turning point?
recall.a: When surplus labour runs out and agricultural wages start to rise; China reached it around 2010-12.

recall.q: Why are ideas special in endogenous growth?
recall.a: They are non-rival, so many firms can use one at once, which breaks diminishing returns.

recall.q: What instrument did AJR use for institutions?
recall.a: Settler mortality in colonial territories.

recall.q: What are Rodrik's conditions for industrial policy to work?
recall.a: Subsidies temporary and tied to performance, bureaucrats autonomous but accountable, and credible withdrawal from failing firms.

sections.title: Agriculture & Rural Livelihoods
sections.big_idea: Farming holds **45% of the workforce on 15% of GDP**, so land, credit, climate and policy decide the fate of the poorest.
in_plain_words: Most holdings are small, land is highly concentrated and about 40% of rural households are functionally landless. Land reform worked where states pushed it, as in West Bengal and Kerala, and stalled where landowners ran state governments. The Green Revolution raised output and left problems of groundwater, soil and debt.

Rural credit fails through adverse selection, moral hazard and weak enforcement, so the poor borrow from moneylenders at high rates. Climate adds heat, erratic monsoons and falling water tables. **MSP, subsidies and insurance mostly reach the irrigated belts**, and tenants and landless labourers fall outside schemes like PM-KISAN.

key_terms.meaning: Government price floor for 23 crops, effective mostly for wheat and rice.
High-yielding varieties behind the Green Revolution; they need irrigation.
Small farms produce more per hectare than large ones.
West Bengal's 1978 tenancy reform that registered tenants.
NABARD programme linking self-help groups to banks through joint liability.

worked_example.title: Output per worker, farm and non-farm
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's figures: agriculture is 15% of GDP and 45% of the workforce. The rest of the economy is therefore 85% of GDP and 55% of workers.
steps: Farm output for each unit of workforce share: 15 ÷ 45 = 0.333.
Non-farm output for each unit of workforce share: 85 ÷ 55 = 1.545.
Compare the two: 1.545 ÷ 0.333 = 4.64.
worked_example.answer: On these shares, output per worker outside farming is about 4.6 times output per worker in farming.

mistakes: Treating all farmers as one group. Holdings, tenure and irrigation differ, and 86% of holdings are marginal or small.
Assuming MSP helps most farmers. The slide says it is effective mostly for wheat and rice in a few states.
Crediting the Green Revolution with gains only. Groundwater, soil and debt costs came with it.
Reading PM-KISAN as reaching the poorest in agriculture. It goes to landowning farmers.

recall.q: Why did land reform stall in India?
recall.a: Land is a state subject, and landowning elites dominated state governments.

recall.q: Which three failures define rural credit markets?
recall.a: Adverse selection, moral hazard and enforcement failure.

recall.q: What did Operation Barga show?
recall.a: Registering tenants raised productivity by 30% or more and reduced poverty.

recall.q: Why does climate stress push groundwater use up?
recall.a: Stress on surface water leads farmers to pump more, which speeds depletion of aquifers.

recall.q: How many crops does MSP cover?
recall.a: Twenty-three.

sections.title: Human Capital: Education & Health
sections.big_idea: Schooling and health are high-return investments, yet **markets under-invest** and India's learning and nutrition lag.
in_plain_words: Each extra year of schooling raises earnings by 8 to 10% on average, and social returns are higher still. Credit failures, information gaps, externalities and child labour explain why households and markets under-invest. India's enrolment is 96%, yet 43% of Grade 3 children cannot read a Grade 1 text.

Health is capital too, and the first 1,000 days matter most. Stunting has fallen to 29.3% while public health spending is 1.84% of GDP. The evidence table ranks interventions, with early nutrition and Teaching at the Right Level near the top. **Returns are highest early in life**, as Heckman's equation shows.

diagram.caption: investments the deck ranks by evidence

key_terms.meaning: Skills, knowledge and health in people that raise their productive capacity.
Teaching at the Right Level: grouping children by what they can do.
Annual survey of rural learning outcomes run by Pratham.
Conception to age 2, when early shocks leave lasting effects.
Health costs paid directly by households; 55M pushed into poverty yearly.

worked_example.title: Schooling returns and the learning gap
worked_example.setup: Illustrative figures: a worker earns Rs 10,000 a month and a Grade 3 class has 40 children. The rates come from the deck.
steps: One more year of schooling raises earnings by 8% to 10% on average.
Low end: 10,000 × 0.08 = 800 rupees a month.
High end: 10,000 × 0.10 = 1,000 rupees a month.
ASER 2022: 43% of Grade 3 children cannot read a Grade 1 text, so 40 × 0.43 = 17.2, about 17 children.
worked_example.answer: A gain of Rs 800 to 1,000 a month, and about 17 of 40 children unable to read at Grade 1 level.

mistakes: Equating enrolment with learning. India has 96% enrolment and a persistent learning crisis.
Taking the deworming result at face value. Attendance gains are strong and test score effects are ambiguous.
Assuming income growth alone fixes malnutrition. Sanitation, women's status and diet matter.
Leaving investment late. Remediation costs far more than prevention in the early years.

recall.q: What share of Grade 3 children cannot read a Grade 1 text (ASER 2022)?
recall.a: 43%, down from 58% in 2012.

recall.q: What is Teaching at the Right Level?
recall.a: Pratham's approach of grouping children by ability and teaching at their level, with learning gains of 0.3 to 0.7 SD.

recall.q: Why do markets under-invest in education?
recall.a: Credit failures, information failures, uncaptured externalities and the child labour opportunity cost.

recall.q: What does India's Human Capital Index of 0.49 mean?
recall.a: A child born today will be 49% as productive as with full education and health.

recall.q: Name the three tiers of India's primary health system.
recall.a: Sub-Centre, Primary Health Centre and Community Health Centre.

sections.title: Credit, Finance & Markets
sections.big_idea: Finance lets the poor smooth shocks and invest a little, but **it enables and does not transform**.
in_plain_words: Financial inclusion covers savings, credit, insurance and payments. India built the JAM stack and UPI, which cut leakage and made payments cheap. Access is different from use, since 40% of Jan Dhan accounts hold zero balance, and biometric authentication can exclude eligible people.

Microfinance helps with consumption smoothing, yet six RCTs found it did not transform poverty. The poor also face risk, where household-level risk can be pooled and region-wide risk cannot. Market failures from public goods to coordination justify intervention, provided you also weigh the failures of government.

key_terms.meaning: Risk hitting everyone at once, such as drought; it cannot be pooled locally.
Risk hitting one household, which neighbours can help pool.
Index insurance pays by an index, which may miss your actual loss.
Jan Dhan, Aadhaar and Mobile: India's delivery stack for transfers.
Illiquid saving that shields money from pressure to share or spend.

worked_example.title: Access is not use
worked_example.setup: The deck says 530 million Jan Dhan accounts were opened by 2023 and 40% hold zero balance.
steps: Zero-balance accounts: 530 × 0.40 = 212 million.
Accounts holding a balance: 530 − 212 = 318 million.
Share with a balance: 318 ÷ 530 = 0.6.
worked_example.answer: About 212 million accounts are empty and 318 million hold a balance, so access does not equal use.

mistakes: Counting accounts opened as people using finance. 40% of Jan Dhan accounts have zero balance.
Expecting microfinance to transform poverty. The RCT evidence shows access and smoothing without a large income change.
Treating index insurance as full cover. A payout can miss the farm's actual loss.
Relying on informal insurance for drought, flood or price shocks. Village networks cannot pool them.

recall.q: What does JAM stand for?
recall.a: Jan Dhan, Aadhaar and Mobile.

recall.q: How do idiosyncratic and covariate risk differ?
recall.a: Idiosyncratic risk hits one household and can be pooled locally; covariate risk hits everyone at once and cannot.

recall.q: What did the six microfinance RCTs find?
recall.a: More credit access and consumption smoothing, with no transformation of poverty levels or incomes.

recall.q: What happened in Andhra Pradesh in 2010?
recall.a: Rapid expansion and aggressive recovery led to farmer suicides, suspended collections and tighter regulation.

recall.q: Why do the poor prefer illiquid savings?
recall.a: They shield savings from social pressure to share and from their own temptation to spend.

sections.title: Trade, Globalisation & Institutions
sections.big_idea: Trade, aid, investment and debt can help or harm, and **who gains depends on domestic institutions and labour markets**.
in_plain_words: Comparative advantage explains gains from trade, and East Asia shows an export route to growth. The elephant curve shows winners in emerging economies and losers among rich-country workers. India has high tariffs and strong services exports but no mass manufacturing, so trade policy links to jobs.

Aid works best in health and humanitarian settings and weakly as budget support. FDI needs absorptive capacity. The Bretton Woods institutions face critiques of governance and conditionality, and sovereign debt can squeeze budgets. Rodrik's trilemma says **deep globalisation, sovereignty and democratic politics cannot all be had at once**.

children.label: Aid
items: Strong in health and humanitarian use

key_terms.meaning: Gain from specialising where relative opportunity cost is lower.
Trade creates winners and losers, depending on factor abundance and labour markets.
Milanovic's picture of who gained from globalisation, 1988-2008.
Aid to one budget line can free money for other spending.
Educated workers and institutions needed to turn FDI into spillovers.

worked_example.title: Who has the comparative advantage?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: in one day Country A makes either 10 cloth or 5 rice, and Country B makes either 2 cloth or 2 rice. A is better at both goods.
steps: A gives up cloth for each rice: 10 ÷ 5 = 2.
B gives up cloth for each rice: 2 ÷ 2 = 1.
B has the lower opportunity cost of rice.
A gives up rice for each cloth: 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5.
B gives up rice for each cloth: 2 ÷ 2 = 1.
worked_example.answer: A specialises in cloth and B in rice, even though A is better at both goods.

mistakes: Assuming liberalisation helps every worker. With segmented labour markets, outcomes can be regressive.
Treating the aid debate as all or nothing. Humanitarian and health aid have strong evidence and budget support is weaker.
Assuming FDI brings benefits automatically. They depend on absorptive capacity.
Taking the Chinese debt-trap story as proven. The slide calls the evidence mixed and points to project design failures.

recall.q: What does comparative advantage say?
recall.a: Gain comes from specialising in goods with lower relative opportunity cost, even if one country is better at everything.

recall.q: Who were the winners and losers in the elephant curve?
recall.a: Winners: the global middle class in emerging economies and the global top 1%. Losers: the rich-country working class.

recall.q: What is fungibility of aid?
recall.a: Aid to one budget line can let governments shift other spending, so the net effect is smaller than the gross aid.

recall.q: Why does IMF governance draw criticism?
recall.a: Voting shares follow economic size, which gives the US effective veto power; India holds 2.6%.

recall.q: What is Rodrik's trilemma?
recall.a: Deep globalisation, national sovereignty and democratic politics cannot all be had at once.

sections.title: Evidence, RCTs & Policy
sections.big_idea: RCTs, natural experiments and political economy each answer a different question: **what works, why, and whether it gets adopted**.
in_plain_words: Randomisation makes treatment and control groups comparable on everything, seen or unseen, so the difference in outcomes is the average treatment effect. RCTs cannot say why a programme works, whether it travels, or how to answer big structural questions, so the deck asks you to pair them with institutional analysis.

When randomisation is impossible, instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity and matching use natural variation. Good policies still fail when small organised groups outweigh diffuse ones, or when local elites capture programmes. **Map who holds power over implementation** before you design.

left.title: What RCTs give
items: Average treatment effect free of selection bias

key_terms.meaning: Random assignment to treatment and control groups to identify causal effects.
Average treatment effect: mean outcome difference between treatment and control.
Exogenous variation that affects treatment but not the outcome directly.
Compares the change over time in treated and control groups.
Local elites taking benefits designed for the poor.

worked_example.title: A difference-in-differences estimate
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: an employment index is 100 at the start in both a treated and a control district. Afterwards the treated district is at 112 and the control district at 106.
steps: Treated change: 112 − 100 = 12.
Control change: 106 − 100 = 6.
The control change stands in for what would have happened anyway.
Difference-in-differences: 12 − 6 = 6.
worked_example.answer: The programme effect is 6 index points, after subtracting the control district's change.

mistakes: Treating an RCT result as true everywhere. External validity and scale effects can change it.
Reading an ATE as an explanation. RCTs show effect size without mechanism.
Designing a programme without asking who controls implementation and who can capture the benefits.
Assuming questions that cannot be randomised have no evidence. Natural experiments answer many of them.

recall.q: What problem does randomisation solve?
recall.a: Selection bias: people who got a programme differ systematically from those who did not.

recall.q: Name the four quasi-experimental methods on slide 70.
recall.a: Instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity and matching.

recall.q: Which years went with the two Nobel Prizes in the section?
recall.a: 2019 for Banerjee, Duflo and Kremer, and 2021 for Card, Angrist and Imbens.

recall.q: What is the Olson logic?
recall.a: Small organised groups lobby effectively, while large diffuse groups face collective action problems.

recall.q: Give two limits of RCTs from the deck.
recall.a: Any two of: external validity, general equilibrium effects, mechanism blindness, ethics, exclusion of structural questions.

sections.title: South Asia Deep Dive
sections.big_idea: South Asia runs from success stories to collapse, and **caste, migration, cities, tribal land and digital access** each add a layer.
in_plain_words: The six-country table shows how far apart the region is, from Bangladesh's garment and female-employment story to Sri Lanka's 2022 crisis. Caste works as an economic institution in jobs, credit and occupations. Climate and the SDG index frame the region's exposure and its data gaps.

Within India, migrants carry parts of the economy but lose entitlements when they move. Cities add productivity yet lack infrastructure money. The Northeast and Adivasi communities face displacement and weak forest rights. Digital infrastructure helps those who can use it, so **inclusion needs non-digital support** too.

key_terms.meaning: COP27 fund for vulnerable countries hit by climate impacts they did not cause.
2006 law recognising forest rights; implementation has fallen short.
Carrying PDS rations, MGNREGS rights or insurance across states.
Open rails such as UPI, ONDC and ABDM on which services build.
Quotas in public jobs and education that miss the private sector.

worked_example.title: The urban infrastructure gap
worked_example.setup: The deck says India spends $17 per urban resident a year on infrastructure, against $100 or more needed. The city size in the last step is illustrative.
steps: Gap per resident: 100 − 17 = 83 dollars.
Share of the need being met: 17 ÷ 100 = 0.17, or 17%.
A city of 1,000,000 residents faces a gap of 1,000,000 × 83 = 83,000,000 dollars a year.
worked_example.answer: At least $83 a resident each year is missing, with only 17% of the need met.

mistakes: Treating South Asia as one story. The deck's lesson is that context specificity is everything.
Reading reservations as a full answer to caste discrimination. They do not cover the private and informal sectors.
Assuming a law on paper means rights on the ground. Only about 3.5 million of 10 million-plus forest claims were settled.
Using migration data as current. The last full migration data is the 2011 Census.

recall.q: Which South Asian country ranks lowest on HDI in the table?
recall.a: Pakistan, at 164.

recall.q: What did Thorat and Attewell find?
recall.a: Identical CVs with upper-caste names got about 1.5 times as many favourable responses as Dalit names.

recall.q: How many lifetime internal migrants did Census 2011 count?
recall.a: 455 million.

recall.q: What was India's urban share in 2023, and when does it cross 50%?
recall.a: 36%, crossing 50% by about 2047.

recall.q: What did the COP27 agreement create?
recall.a: A Loss and Damage fund.

sections.title: Contemporary Challenges
sections.big_idea: Jobs, automation, democracy, inequality and ecological limits are the live questions, and **eight practitioner questions** turn theory into design.
in_plain_words: India's central contradiction is jobless growth: 7 to 10 million new workers a year against 3 to 4 million formal jobs. AI and automation may close the labour-intensive route. Inequality has risen, with the top 1% income share at 22.6%. Democracy's link to growth is unresolved, and Sen treats it as part of development itself.

Planetary boundaries add an ecological ceiling. Theory of change, cost-effectiveness analysis and the eight questions turn evidence into design: market failure, counterfactual, beneficiaries, evidence, power, measurement, side effects and scale-up. Informality, state capacity, care, decentralisation and rights are the extra lenses. **Use CEA as one input** among several.

diagram.caption: the doughnut: development between a floor and a ceiling

key_terms.meaning: GDP growth without enough jobs, as India's capital-intensive growth shows.
Returns to capital exceed growth, so wealth concentrates over time.
Nine biophysical limits for safe human activity; six are crossed.
Map of causal pathways from activities to long-run impact.
Disability-Adjusted Life Year: one year of healthy life lost.

worked_example.title: Inequality arithmetic
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's figures for India's top 1% income share and for Piketty's r > g illustration.
steps: The top 1% share rose from 10.5% in 1990 to 22.6%: 22.6 − 10.5 = 12.1 percentage points.
As a multiple: 22.6 ÷ 10.5 = 2.15, so the share roughly doubled.
Billionaire wealth growing at 15% a year against GDP at 7%: 15 − 7 = 8 points faster each year.
worked_example.answer: The share rose 12.1 points, about 2.15 times, and billionaire wealth outpaced GDP by 8 points a year on the slide's figures.

mistakes: Using cost-effectiveness analysis as the only decision rule. It favours what is easy to measure.
Treating a pilot's success as proof of success at scale.
Blaming weak delivery on money alone. The slide names implementation capacity at district and block level.
Designing women's empowerment schemes that ignore care burdens.

recall.q: How many planetary boundaries have been crossed?
recall.a: Six of the nine.

recall.q: What are the 3Fs of effective decentralisation?
recall.a: Functions, functionaries and funds.

recall.q: What does the 3R framework propose for unpaid care?
recall.a: Recognise, reduce and redistribute.

recall.q: What cost per DALY threshold does the deck give for India?
recall.a: One to three times GDP per capita, about $2,500 to $7,500.

recall.q: What are the first two of the eight practitioner questions?
recall.a: What is the market failure? Who is the counterfactual?

notes.2: Use the agenda as the **map for the course**. It lists eleven sections plus a further reading block, each with slide ranges. Sections 10 and 11 also pull in slides placed later in the deck, so follow the slide numbers given and skip strict page order.
notes.4: The core question is why some countries grow rich and others stay poor. Remember the field's habits: it **mixes macro with micro**, takes context seriously and leans on experiments and surveys. Keep the definition box as your one-sentence answer when someone asks what the field is.
notes.5: Read the table as a list of assumptions that fail. Standard economics expects working markets and symmetric information, while here **markets are missing, thin or distorted**. The warning at the bottom is practical: assume working credit and enforced contracts in a district and you will misdiagnose it.
notes.6: Match each thinker to one idea and the slide sticks. Sen: capabilities. Lewis: surplus labour leaving agriculture. Banerjee and Duflo: **randomised trials**. Ray: the canonical textbook. Bardhan: India's political economy. Drèze with Sen: public action and rights.
notes.7: Three traditions answer one question differently: structure and institutions, experiments, and capabilities. A useful test is to ask **what each would measure**: sectors and rules, programme effects, or freedoms. The closing line says no single tradition is enough, so expect later slides to borrow from all three.
notes.8: Sen defines development by freedoms, and the box beneath translates it. Average income can rise while people stay ill, unschooled or voiceless. Take away the closing questions and **ask them of every programme**: who can actually access benefits, and whose freedoms are growing?
notes.10: GDP per capita is the default because it is easy to compare, and the two lists show where it helps and where it is blind. Remember the pair **distribution and unpaid work**. The India case closes the slide: growth above 7% while female labour participation fell.
notes.11: The HDI takes a geometric mean of health, education and income. Its Bangladesh paradox is the memory hook: **a lower income than Pakistan until about 2020, yet a higher HDI**. Compare India's income rank with its HDI rank to see the gap the slide calls underinvestment.
notes.12: Every poverty line is a choice. The table lists lines for different purposes, so ask **which line, set by whom, for what use** before you quote a number. PPP makes countries comparable. The data-gap box matters: India's last comparable consumption survey is 2011-12.
notes.13: Read the four tiles as one story: a fall from 36% to 8.5%, a COVID setback of 70 million, and 690 million still in extreme poverty. The China box says much of the fall came from one country, so **always ask what the trend looks like without China**.
notes.14: The MPI counts people deprived in at least one-third of the weighted indicators at the same time. Remember the structure: health, education and living standards each carry one-third. The lesson for programmes is that **income targeting misses deprivation**, so several sectors must work together.
notes.15: The Gini runs from 0 for perfect equality to 1 for one person owning everything, and the Lorenz curve shows the gap behind it. **Compare the income and wealth Ginis**: India's 0.35 and 0.63 describe very different concentrations of land, financial assets and business ownership.
notes.16: This table is the whole section on one page. Each metric comes with its producer and its limit, so read the limit column first. The practitioner principle is the takeaway: **triangulate** income, deprivation, distribution and qualitative evidence, and distrust any single-number claim about progress.
notes.18: A poverty trap is a loop with a threshold. The S-curve crosses the 45 degree line three times: a poor equilibrium, an unstable threshold and a rich equilibrium. Below the threshold you slide back and above it you climb, which is why **a one-time push across the threshold** can last.
notes.19: Kuznets predicted that inequality rises and then falls as countries develop. The slide lists cases that break the pattern: China and India, Korea and Taiwan, Bangladesh. The modern view is that **high inequality weakens growth** through human capital, instability and institutions. Look for the missing inverted U in the scatter.
notes.20: This slide moves poverty from income to experience. The four boxes, material deprivation, voicelessness, vulnerability and social exclusion, give you **a vocabulary for what people describe**. The quotation rests on interviews with 60,000 people in 60 countries, so use it when someone asks why income is not enough.
notes.21: Rural poverty here has recognisable faces: landless labourers, marginal farmers, SC and ST households, women-headed households, seasonal migrants and Adivasi communities. Learn them as **overlapping disadvantages**. The key insight says a programme that ignores caste, gender, land and geography will miss the poorest.
notes.22: Follow the four boxes as a loop across two generations. The numbers compare India's 0.52 income elasticity with the Nordic 0.15, and **a higher figure means a child's income tracks the parent's more closely**. One-off interventions that leave nutrition, schooling and credit untouched will fade.
notes.23: Use this slide to see where poverty sits. Six high-burden states hold over half of India's poor with about 40% of the population. The data-gap box warns that **comparison with 2011-12 is blocked** by the suppressed 2017-18 survey and the changed 2022-23 method.
notes.24: The slide gives five channels: wages, assets, unpaid care, unequal sharing inside households and restricted mobility. Household poverty figures hide the fourth. The Bangladesh contrast is the hope: female participation above 40% shows that **shifts in labour demand can move outcomes quickly**.
notes.25: Read the table row by row as instrument, mechanism, Indian programme and evidence. The pattern in the last column is that **leakage fell, while quality and coverage stay uneven**. Note that the slide records MGNREGA being replaced from 1 July 2026, with a 125-day guarantee. End on the UBI debate.
notes.27: Solow says capital piles up with diminishing returns until a steady state, and only technology lifts the long-run rate. Remember the residual: **50 to 70% of growth in rich countries** is unexplained by capital and labour. A higher saving rate raises the level of output but not the long-run growth rate.
notes.28: Lewis pictured two sectors: a traditional one with surplus labour and a modern one that reinvests profits. Development is labour moving across. Watch for the **turning point**, when farm wages start to rise. China reached it around 2010-12, and India has probably not, having gone from farms to services.
notes.29: Read the chart in three eras: about 3.5% under the Hindu rate, 6.4% after 1991, and a 5.8% fall in 2020. The tension is **growth without jobs**, because the growth was capital and skill intensive. Treat the pre-COVID slowdown from 8.2% to 4% as a separate question from the pandemic.
notes.30: Solow let technology fall from the sky, and Romer and Lucas made it the result of investment. The hook is that **ideas are non-rival**: one blueprint serves everyone at once, which breaks diminishing returns. Bangalore shows the limit, with under 4 million workers in a labour force above 500 million.
notes.31: Know the ten pillars by name, because later slides argue against them. The 'what went wrong' list gives four counter-examples. Take away Rodrik's post-consensus view: **diagnose the binding constraint in each context**. India's 1991 reforms were only partly Washington Consensus, so judge them as a mixture.
notes.32: The settler mortality argument runs in a chain: high mortality led to extractive institutions, low mortality to inclusive ones, and both persist. The India examples show that **institutional design matters as well as rules**. The last box adds that a weak state with good rules is still a weak state.
notes.33: The table compares two models on growth engine, structure, poverty, state role, human capital and income. Learn the key lesson row: **China built human capital, land reform and state capacity before the market took off**, while India liberalised without that base. The closing paragraph says Sen and Panagariya may both be right.
notes.34: Industrial policy is back. Rodrik's three conditions give you a test: subsidies **temporary and tied to performance**, bureaucrats autonomous but accountable, and a state able to withdraw support from failing firms. The slide says the Licence Raj failed all three. None of today's schemes targets labour-intensive sectors.
notes.36: Agriculture is 15% of GDP and 45% of the workforce, so it still carries the poor. Pair the Ravallion and Chen result, that farm growth cuts poverty two to three times faster, with the **productivity paradox** of very productive and very unproductive areas in one country. The suicide figure is attributed to structural causes.
notes.37: Land is the root asset: it shapes income, status, credit and power. West Bengal and Kerala show that reform can work. The slide names why it stalled: **land is a state subject**, and landowning elites dominated state governments. The barrier it names is political economy.
notes.38: The Green Revolution was a technology that worked and left costs. Sort the points into two columns: gains in wheat, rice and food prices, and shadows in groundwater, soil, monoculture and debt. Ask **who had irrigation and credit**, because they gained most. The closing debate points to eastern India.
notes.39: Three failures explain why banks avoid the rural poor: adverse selection, moral hazard and weak enforcement. Match each to the four listed barriers. The consequence is **moneylender interest of 36 to 120%**, which feeds the poverty trap. SHG linkage helps, though the slide calls its effect modest.
notes.40: South Asian farming is exposed on heat, monsoon, groundwater and livestock. Spot the feedback loop: **climate stress pushes farmers to pump more groundwater**, which speeds depletion. The slide ends by putting adaptation first for farmers, since mitigation offers no near-term relief.
notes.41: Each row is an instrument paired with its critique. The pattern to remember is that **benefits flow to irrigated belts and landowners**, while tenants and labourers are left out, as with PM-KISAN. Read the critique column before you judge any scheme, then use the farm law paragraph as an example of contested reform.
notes.43: Human capital is the stock of skills and health in people. The private return of 8 to 10% per extra year of schooling understates the social return. The four reasons markets under-invest give you **a checklist for justifying public subsidy**. Enrolment of 96% sits beside 43% of Grade 3 children unable to read.
notes.44: Enrolment is near universal, yet learning lags. Read the percentages together: 43% of Grade 3 children cannot read a Grade 1 text, down from 58% in 2012. The four causes lead to one fix, **Teaching at the Right Level**, which groups children by ability. Ask whether a school teaches at the child's level.
notes.45: Health is capital too. Hold two stories: the Worm Wars, where the evidence on deworming is contested, and the **first 1,000 days**, where early shocks scar adult earnings. Then read the four numbers as signs of underinvestment, including public health spending of 1.84% of GDP.
notes.46: The paradox is surplus food alongside widespread stunting. The four explanations for why growth alone does not fix nutrition are sanitation, women's status, dietary diversity and the farm-nutrition mismatch. Remember that **sanitation is a nutrition intervention**. Compare stunting's fall from 48% to 29.3% with the slower POSHAN progress.
notes.47: The Human Capital Index measures how much of their potential a child born today will reach by age 18. India scores 0.49, so about **half of productive potential is lost** to preventable gaps. Use the chart to compare regions. Bangladesh scores 0.46, just below India and above Pakistan's 0.41.
notes.48: India's primary care runs in three tiers, and the table gives the population norm for each. The second half is the gap between norm and reality in buildings, staff and drugs, with **ASHA workers holding the system together**. Treat the Health and Wellness Centres as an ambition with uneven delivery.
notes.49: This table ranks interventions by strength of evidence. Early nutrition and Teaching at the Right Level carry the largest effects, and deworming is contested on learning. The Heckman point is the rule: **returns are highest early and fall with age**, so prevention costs less than remediation.
notes.50: Education, health and income reinforce one another in both directions. Read the four arrows and notice that two need **public goods to break the credit constraint** or can be cut by labour market failures. Kerala is the proof: high literacy and health first, then the highest HDI in India.
notes.52: Financial inclusion means savings, credit, insurance and payments, and JAM is India's delivery route. The distinction to hold is access versus use: **40% of Jan Dhan accounts hold zero balance**. Keep the leakage savings and the exclusion errors in view together, because one system does both.
notes.53: Microfinance began with group liability solving adverse selection and moral hazard. Six RCTs found **more credit access and smoother consumption, with no transformation of poverty**. The Andhra Pradesh crisis of 2010 brought tighter regulation. Hold both halves: it does useful things and cannot replace public investment.
notes.54: Split risk into two kinds. Idiosyncratic risk hits one household and a village can pool it; covariate risk hits everyone at once and cannot be pooled. The **anti-insurance trap** is when coping, such as selling assets or pulling children from school, deepens poverty. Government transfers fill the gap formal insurance leaves.
notes.55: UPI shows digital public infrastructure at work: open, interoperable rails on which private firms build. The tiles give scale, over 14 billion transactions a month and a zero merchant fee. Then read the inclusion question, because **the poorest are still excluded or pay intermediaries**.
notes.56: Learn the six failures from the table: public goods, externalities, information asymmetry, missing markets, coordination failures and natural monopoly. Rodrik's question replaces 'more state or more market?' with **which failure, which instrument, at what cost**. Government failures belong in the same comparison.
notes.57: Portfolios of the Poor documented how poor households really manage money. The hook is **8 to 10 instruments at once** and a preference for illiquid savings that shield money from pressure to share. The central problem is 'lumping' small flows into lump sums. Commitment devices can raise saving without higher income.
notes.58: This synthesis lists what finance can and cannot do. Compare the two columns line by line. The sentence to remember is the last one: **finance enables; it does not transform**. Structural change in labour markets, health systems and institutions still drives development in aggregate.
notes.60: Comparative advantage says gains come from specialising in what costs less in opportunity terms. Stolper-Samuelson warns of losers when labour markets are segmented. The India dilemma closes the slide: IT services fit the theory, but **manufacturing creates mass employment**, so trade, jobs and industrial policy are linked.
notes.61: The elephant curve shows who gained between 1988 and 2008: the global middle class in emerging economies and the global top 1%. The squeezed group was the rich-country working class. Add **slowbalisation**, the plateau in trade share since about 2008, which may narrow the export route East Asia used.
notes.62: Set Sachs's Big Push against Moyo's call to phase out aid, then read the evidence block. It says **the effect of aid depends on its type**: humanitarian and health aid have strong evidence, budget support much weaker. Fungibility means aid can free money for other spending. The 2024 box warns about abrupt cuts.
notes.63: FDI can bring capital, technology and export access, but the slide says the benefits are not automatic. Pair the benefits with the concerns. The condition that decides the outcome is **absorptive capacity**: educated workers and strong institutions. Use the chart and the $71B peak to judge India's scale.
notes.64: Read the table as institution, mandate, role and critique. The critique column is the useful one for practitioners. The paragraph below explains governance asymmetry: voting weights follow economic size, so the US holds effective veto power. India's 2.6% IMF vote share makes the point.
notes.65: Debt is a tool when returns beat borrowing costs and a trap when shocks hit. Check the four country tiles, then the Chinese debt question. The slide calls the evidence mixed and gives **four reasons the 'trap' story is incomplete**. Its closing line blames design failure in development finance.
notes.66: This slide ties the section together country by country: Bangladesh's garment concentration, India's services strength, fragile Nepal and Sri Lanka, Pakistan, and stalled SAARC trade. Keep Rodrik's trilemma as the frame: deep globalisation, sovereignty and democracy cannot all be had, so **say which you are choosing**.
notes.68: RCTs randomise treatment so the groups are comparable on everything, seen or unseen. The difference in outcomes is the average treatment effect, and the gain is **no selection bias**. The last paragraph lists findings that changed policy, from deworming to bed nets. Try to state the lesson of each.
notes.69: The quotation sums up the critique: RCTs say what worked here, and cannot say why or elsewhere. Sort the six limits into groups: **validity** (external validity, scale), **scope** (questions you cannot randomise, structural barriers) and **ethics and mechanism**. The synthesis pairs RCTs with structural analysis.
notes.70: Four quasi-experimental methods: IV, difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity and matching. For each, learn the logic in one line and one example. The Indian natural experiments below show **how history, trade and politics can be studied without randomising**. The slide ends by moving from what works to what scales.
notes.71: Good policy still fails when power is uneven. Olson's logic says small organised groups lobby well and large diffuse groups do not. Elite capture follows predictably. Use the four India studies as examples, and take the practitioner rule: **map who controls implementation** before you design.
notes.73: The table compares six countries on income, HDI rank, poverty and story. Read one line per country and keep the pattern: a dynamic India, Bangladesh's success, a stalled Pakistan and Sri Lanka's collapse. The lesson is **context specificity**, since the range within the region rivals the range across continents.
notes.74: Caste operates as an economic institution in jobs, credit, occupations and networks. The Thorat and Attewell result is the number to keep: identical CVs got **about 1.5 times as many favourable responses** with upper-caste names. Reservations built an SC and ST middle class but do not cover the private and informal sectors.
notes.75: Cities raise productivity, and urban wages are 50 to 100% higher than rural ones for comparable workers. The problem is under-planning and thin city finance: $17 per resident against $100+ needed. Read the tiles as **400 million more urban residents by 2050** that infrastructure and property tax must meet.
notes.76: Climate is framed as a justice issue: high vulnerability and low responsibility. Use the four tiles for scale and the four nexus bullets for channels: agriculture, water, coasts and labour. The loss and damage fund is the policy hook, and the closing line says **delivery remains far from need**.
notes.77: Read the SDG index as a score out of 100: 71 now, up from 57 in 2018. Split the goals into the on-track and laggard lists. Hunger, health, gender, inequality and institutions lag. The data-gap warning is the practical point: **you cannot track what you cannot measure**.
notes.79: Jobless growth is the contradiction: 7 to 10 million new workers a year against 3 to 4 million formal jobs. The slide ties it to capital-intensive growth and a manufacturing share stuck near 17% of GDP. It reads falling participation as **discouraged workers leaving** a market with no acceptable options.
notes.80: Automation could close the labour-intensive path that East Asia took. Acemoglu's point is that the direction of AI follows policy choices on R&D, IP and tax. Sort the rest into opportunity (talent, public digital platforms, health, farming, education) and risk (reskilling speed, **no protection for informal workers**, creative livelihoods).
notes.81: Four positions on democracy and development: the case for, the case for complexity, India's evidence and Sen's answer. Hold the tension that the growth correlation is near zero in aggregate. Then take Sen's resolution: democracy is **both a tool for development and part of what development means**.
notes.82: Piketty's r > g explains why wealth concentrates. The India tiles show the top 1% income share rising from 10.5% in 1990 to 22.6%. Read the 'particularly bad' paragraph for the combination of factors, and the **Piketty paradox** at the end: the conditions that create extreme inequality also protect it.
notes.83: Planetary boundaries set an ecological ceiling and the doughnut adds a social floor. The development dilemma is that rich countries crossed the boundaries and now ask others to grow differently. The South Asian list covers pollution, water, forests and soil. **Green GDP** asks what growth looks like after subtracting degradation.
notes.84: Use these ten ideas as a **checklist for the whole course**. Group them: context and institutions (1, 2), markets and human capital (3, 4), poverty and distribution (5, 6), politics and evidence (7, 8), and climate and politics (9, 10). Link each to a section before moving on.
notes.85: This is a source list for finding credible evidence. Split it into journals, open databases and research organisations. Start with the databases for numbers and the organisations for evidence summaries. **Record which source each figure came from**, as the deck does on its slides.
notes.86: Internal migration is called India's largest and least-studied transformation. Hold three facts: 455 million lifetime migrants, 30 to 40 million returning in the first lockdown, and entitlements that do not travel. The barriers are caste networks and **no portability of PDS, MGNREGS and insurance**. One Nation One Ration Card is a partial fix.
notes.87: Read the tiles for scale and for gaps: 900 million users, but 33% of them female and rural penetration of 45% against 78% urban. The four public infrastructure items show the design bet. The closing caveat is the lesson: **benefits flow to those who can use the tools**, so inclusion needs non-digital investment.
notes.88: This slide covers groups that standard analysis overlooks. The Forest Rights Act recognised rights on paper, yet only about 3.5 million of 10 million-plus claims were settled. Displacement, conflict and the Siliguri Corridor shape the Northeast. Sikkim's organic status is the **bright spot to remember**.
notes.89: A theory of change maps inputs to outputs, outcomes and impact. Use the five inputs as questions: market failure, mechanism evidence, political economy, counterfactual and scale-up. **Write the chain first, then test each link** against the evidence. The slide points to the MEL course for the workbench.
notes.90: Cost-effectiveness analysis ranks interventions by impact per rupee. A DALY is a year of healthy life lost, and the WHO threshold is one to three times GDP per capita. Use the benchmark table to compare orders of magnitude, and keep CEA as **one input among several** when you decide.
notes.91: The slide puts informal employment above 90% and the informal share of GDP at about 50%. Learn the four reasons it persists: regulation, weak enforcement, capital costs and demonetisation. The e-Shram portal is a step toward **portable social protection**, though registration does not guarantee benefits.
notes.92: State capacity is framed as the binding constraint. The Bihar and Tamil Nadu contrast shows that **similar schemes and funds give very different outcomes**. Use the five requirements as an audit list: fiscal capacity, bureaucratic quality, information systems, social accountability and district leadership. Pritchett's capability trap warns against adding programmes without capacity.
notes.93: GDP leaves out unpaid care. Women who do this work spend about 5 hours a day on it against men's 1.6. The 3R frame, **recognise, reduce, redistribute**, gives the policy menu. The development implication is a test for any women's empowerment scheme: check whether it addresses childcare before expecting attendance.
notes.94: The 73rd and 74th Amendments set up three tiers of local government. Kerala shows what real devolution delivers, and elsewhere the form exists without the substance. Remember the **3Fs: functions, functionaries, funds**. Without all three a panchayat has authority on paper only.
notes.95: This table lists the legal instruments behind development rights. Pair each with what it guarantees. The theme is the gap between rights and delivery, which the slide blames on state capacity, political economy and missing accountability. PIL shows **courts acting when politics fails**, and the slide calls that no lasting substitute for a working democracy.
notes.96: These eight questions work as a **field checklist**: market failure, counterfactual, beneficiaries, evidence, power, measurement, second-order effects and scale-up. Take a programme you know and answer all eight in writing. Question 3 asks you to disaggregate outcomes, and question 5 asks who can capture the benefits.
notes.97: These six books are the course's reading list. Read them in this order for a path: Sen for the idea, Banerjee and Duflo for the experiments, Sen and Drèze for India, Acemoglu and Robinson for institutions, Piketty for inequality, Rodrik for **how to use models as tools**.
notes.98: Read this chart across countries. Bangladesh overtook Pakistan around 2020 despite a much smaller starting base, and Sri Lanka's 2022 collapse is plain to see. **Single-country charts would hide both stories**, which is why the slide uses a panel.
notes.99: The Sankey follows workforce shares across 1991, 2011 and 2023. Agriculture falls from 60% to about 46% and the flow lands in services. The textbook sequence runs agriculture, manufacturing, services, and here the **manufacturing step is weak**. The slide calls this jobless industrialisation.
notes.100: This is a reading and course list. Group the sources: data and reports first, then the ImpactMojo courses. The flagship course on this topic has 16 modules. **Use the free data sources to check any figure you meet**, such as NFHS-5 and PLFS.
notes.101: A glossary slide for revision. Cover the right-hand column and define each term aloud, then check. The two halves group naturally: measurement terms first, GDP through the Lewis turning point, then evidence and market terms from RCT onward. **Self-test before you finish the course.**
notes.102: Read the sectoral shares as the chart of the Lewis transition. Services rose to about 55%, industry plateaued near 25% and agriculture fell from about 50% to about 17% of GDP while employing about 46% of workers. The gap between **share of output and share of jobs** is the incomplete transition.
notes.103: The MPI chart covers three NFHS rounds. 415 million people exited multidimensional poverty between 2005-06 and 2019-21 and about 231 million remain, mostly in five states. The slide says income poverty shows a similar trajectory, but the **dimensional view shows nutrition, sanitation, electricity and schooling moving together**.
